parts.title: Sentence comprehension: Archive volunteer note
parts.instructions: Read the short email from a friend. Choose the best word for each gap (1-5).
parts.passage:
Hi Salma,

I wanted to tell you how my Saturday mornings at the town archive are going. Although I was nervous about handling fragile maps at first, I soon got [1] to wearing soft cotton gloves. Our head archivist, Beatrice, always reminds us to [2] care when turning old newspaper pages. Last week we sorted a box of nineteenth-century postcards, [3] had been stored in a damp cellar for years. You do not need to bring any stationery because the archive [4] all the pencils and folders. Let me know if you feel like signing [5] for next month's training afternoon!

Best,
Declan

questions.explanation: 'Get used to + -ing' means becoming comfortable with a routine; 'familiar' takes 'with' and 'known' does not fit.
'Take care' is the natural collocation meaning to act carefully; 'make' and 'do' do not collocate with 'care' here.
'Which' introduces a non-defining relative clause referring back to 'a box of nineteenth-century postcards'.
'Supplies all the pencils and folders' means provides them for volunteers; 'attends' and 'contains' do not fit.
'Sign up for' is the phrasal verb meaning to register for an event or training session.

parts.title: Text cohesion: Exploring the old mill

Once we entered the main hall, however, the wide space looked surprisingly bright and empty.
At the stone gate, our guide handed everyone a faded black-and-white photograph showing the building in 1910.
She explained that all the heavy weaving machines had been removed decades ago when the factory closed.

'Before we stepped inside, she pointed out the tall brick chimney...' follows the arrival at the gate and prepares for entering the building.

'She explained that all the heavy weaving machines had been removed...' explains why the main hall looked bright and empty.

parts.title: Opinion matching: Local history walks and archives
parts.instructions: Four people (A-D) give their opinions about local history walks and town archives. Match each statement (1-7) to the correct person. You can use each person more than once.

texts.title: Beatrice
texts.text: I love joining evening history walks around the old quarter because the pavements are much quieter after six o'clock. A good guide can pause safely and point out carved stone faces or old shop signs high above eye level. I never book tours that rush through ten streets in a single hour just to tick off famous buildings. For me, the best walks have small groups where everyone can hear clearly without wearing plastic headphones.

texts.title: Connor
texts.text: For years I assumed our county archive was only open to university professors writing thick history books. That changed completely when I visited last autumn to trace who had built my Victorian terraced house. The staff showed me old street directories and tax maps, and they could not have been more welcoming. My only frustration is that the reading room closes at four on weekdays, which makes it awkward for anyone with a full-time job.

texts.title: Hazel
texts.text: I lead weekend heritage walks for local families, and I always focus on ordinary people rather than kings or politicians. Listeners remember the past far better when they hear what a bakery apprentice earned or how families shared one water pump in the yard. I also believe the town council should install clearer metal plaques on historic street corners so residents can explore the neighbourhood at their own pace anytime.

texts.title: Vikram
texts.text: Most weekends I prefer browsing digitised newspapers and old railway maps on my tablet at home rather than walking behind a flag in a crowded tour group. You can zoom in on tiny details and compare different decades in seconds. Even so, I have to admit that standing beside an actual stone bridge with an experienced guide gives you a real sense of scale that a flat screen simply cannot provide.

parts.title: Long text comprehension: Saving town memories
parts.instructions: Read the article about how local history walks and community archives preserve town heritage. Match each paragraph (1-7) to the best heading (A-H). There is one extra heading that you do not need.

paragraphs.text: Every town carries clues to its past right on its street signs, even when old factories and workshops have long since disappeared. Names like Mill Lane, Tanner Street, or Rope Walk tell walkers exactly what workers once produced in those neighbourhoods centuries ago. Other street names recall lost geography, such as streams that now flow underground in brick pipes or hills that were flattened to build railway stations. When you learn to read these everyday labels, a routine walk to the supermarket turns into a living map of how the community grew and earned its living.

While stone bridges and brick churches can survive for hundreds of years, paper records of daily life are far more fragile. Old shop receipt books, family letters, theatre programmes, and parish newsletters often sit forgotten in damp cellars or hot attics. When a house is cleared after an elderly relative moves away, boxes of priceless local photographs are frequently thrown into rubbish skips before anyone checks what is inside. Once those personal papers are destroyed, historians lose the small details of how ordinary neighbours actually dressed, worked, and spent their free time.

Across the country, volunteer-run community archives are stepping in to rescue these unwanted documents before they vanish. At a typical Saturday session, trained helpers carefully brush away dust with soft goat-hair brushes, remove rusty metal paperclips that stain old paper, and place each item inside acid-free folders. Every photograph or diary is then given a reference number and logged in a simple catalogue. Although the work demands patience, volunteers say that opening a donated shoebox feels like unwrapping a time capsule from their own street.

In the past, anyone wishing to consult an old street directory or census page had to travel to a quiet reading room during weekday office hours. Today, high-resolution scanners allow small archives to photograph fragile pages once and share them online with thousands of residents. Interactive websites now let users lay a Victorian town map directly over a modern satellite view, sliding a bar back and forth to see which orchards became housing estates. Far from reducing interest in physical archives, digital access often inspires online browsers to visit in person.

Archives store the raw evidence, yet guided history walks are what truly bring those dusty facts to life on the pavement. When a local guide stops outside a converted bank or a quiet courtyard, they can hold up a printed copy of an archive photograph from ninety years ago. Standing in the exact spot where horse-drawn carts once unloaded grain makes dates and figures feel real and immediate. Walkers also notice architectural clues—such as blocked-up cellar windows or faded painted advertisements on brick walls—that they had walked past for years without seeing.

Written documents never tell the whole story of a neighbourhood, especially when it comes to dialects, songs, and workplace humour. To fill that gap, many heritage groups now run oral history projects, sitting down with older residents over a cup of tea to record their memories. People in their eighties and nineties can describe what the high street smelled like on market day, how neighbours helped each other during winter storms, or what games children played before television arrived. Stored alongside paper files, these voices add warmth and personality to the town record.

Keeping local heritage alive depends on passing curiosity to the next generation, not just preserving old boxes on shelves. Several towns now partner with secondary schools so teenagers can interview grandparents, research the history of their own school buildings, and design short walking routes for parents. When young people discover that a famous inventor lived two streets away or that their park used to be an airfield, local history stops feeling like a distant subject in a textbook. Instead, it becomes a shared story that belongs to everyone living there today.

Paragraph 2 focuses on how fragile paper records in attics and cellars are often damaged or thrown away during house clearances.

parts.title: Opinion matching: Digital vs. paper archives

turns.text: Oh, completely! We both know searching digital files at home is a huge time-saver compared with checking paper indexes. Still, I don't think digital copies should replace visiting the reading room. Holding a real hundred-year-old letter in your hands feels special in a way a computer screen never will.

If a clear scan gives me the exact same words, I'm quite happy to leave the original safely in a dark box. My only complaint about our local archive is that the website search tool is still rather confusing for beginners.

parts.title: Monologue comprehension
parts.instructions: Listen to two speakers giving short talks: first an archivist about a community photo project (questions 1-2), then a walking-tour guide about leading evening tours (questions 3-4). Choose the best answer for each question.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: First, you will hear Patrick, a town archivist, talking about a project to collect old family photographs.

turns.speaker: patrick
turns.text: When we launched our community photo project last spring, we placed a wooden drop-off box in the town library, expecting a few dozen faded wedding pictures. Within two weeks, local families had brought in over six hundred photographs from attics and shoeboxes! The main reason we asked people to bring them in person, rather than emailing scans, was so our volunteers could sit with each donor and write down the names, streets, and stories behind every image before those memories were forgotten. Without captions, an old photo of a street party is just a crowd of strangers. I expected retired residents to bring the most pictures, and they certainly did. What really surprised me, though, was how many young parents arrived with boxes left behind by grandparents, keen to learn what their own street looked like fifty years ago. Watching three generations gather around one table to identify an old corner shop made all the long Saturday sorting sessions worthwhile.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Now you will hear Alba, a local historian, talking about leading her first guided walking tours.

turns.speaker: alba
turns.text: Before I led my first walking tour three years ago, I spent months reading council records and memorising exact construction dates for every stone bridge and church in the district. I was terrified someone in the group would ask a date I couldn't recall! On my very first walk, though, I realised that visitors don't want a walking history book. The hardest lesson for me wasn't learning how to project my voice outdoors or managing latecomers—it was cutting half my notes so the group had time to look up at the buildings and ask their own questions. Whenever new volunteer guides ask me for advice before starting their own routes, I tell them not to try covering the entire town in ninety minutes. Pick just four or five stops within a short distance, share one vivid human story at each corner, and leave plenty of breathing room for conversation.

To record the names and stories behind them
To avoid receiving too many emails at once
questions.explanation: Patrick explains that bringing photos in person allowed volunteers to sit with donors and write down names, streets, and stories before they were forgotten.

questions.prompt: What surprised Patrick most during the photo project?

How quickly retired residents visited the library
How many young parents brought in family boxes
questions.explanation: Patrick expected retired residents to participate, so what really surprised him was how many young parents arrived with boxes from their grandparents.

Dealing with people who arrived late

questions.explanation: Alba says the hardest lesson was not projecting her voice or managing latecomers, but cutting half her notes so visitors could look around and ask questions.

questions.explanation: Alba advises new guides not to cover the whole town in ninety minutes, and instead to pick just four or five stops close together with one vivid story at each.

parts.title: Compare two photographs
parts.instructions: Look at the two photographs. First describe and compare them (45 seconds), then answer the two numbered questions (45 seconds each).
parts.prompt:
Tell me what you see in these two photographs and compare the two ways of learning about history. Then answer these two questions:
1. What are the advantages of reading books in a quiet historic library compared with visiting historic buildings outdoors on a guided walk?
2. Which of these two ways of learning about local history would you prefer on a weekend, and why?

parts.title: Personal experience and discussion
parts.instructions: You have 1 minute to prepare and 2 minutes to speak continuously. Answer all three questions in one organised talk.

topics.prompt:
Talk about a time when you learned something interesting about the history of a place. Answer all three questions in one 2-minute talk:
1. Tell me about a historic place you visited or researched and what you discovered.
2. How did learning about its past change the way you saw that place?
3. Why is it important for towns to protect old buildings and local archives for future generations?
